relevant_group_routes.relationship: Indigenous and mixed-descent women written into Canadian women's history, with race as a division among women (1980–98)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period. As Bowsfield quotes the book (Archivaria 12, 1981, p. 124; no page given), Van Kirk claimed that it 'supports the claims of theorists in women's history that sex roles should constitute a category of historical investigation', and she admitted the limits of relying on male sources. He finds 'a feminist note to some of Van Kirk's statements but it must be admitted that it is not a strident one'. Gagan and Turner's survey of Canadian social history (Archivaria 14, 1982, p. 29 and n. 7) puts 'Many Tender Ties' and Strangers in Blood under women's work: 'two noteworthy recent studies attempt to recreate the whole way of life of a particular group of "working" women, those who participated in the Canadian fur trade', in which 'the whole woman-wife, mother, labourer, diplomat, chattel, entrepreneur-is revealed'. Her own words, 1986 (Manitoba History 11, read in full): 'Other important themes for women's history also emerge'; 'The reasons for such "unsisterly" action should be confronted squarely by feminist historians'; 'The rivalry among women in nineteenth century Red River, however, was compounded by the issue of race'; and 'The racism evinced by white women in Red River, while as inexcusable as that of their male counterparts, was aggravated by what, in their view, was a concrete threat to their own welfare in the competition for eligible husbands.' 1997–98 (BC Studies 115/116, pp. 149–51 read): 'Little attention has been paid to the fact that this process of acculturation was gendered'; 'a complex interaction of gender and class dynamics, coupled with the particular demographics of early Victoria, enabled the girls to transcend the racist climate of the colony more successfully than the boys' (p. 150). Reception in a Canadian women's studies journal, 2000 (Atlantis 25:1, both read in full): McPherson calls the book a 'now-classic work' and writes that 'Van Kirk's research and the critical debates it has aroused have played a crucial role in writing Native women into western Canadian history and in bringing cultural difference and conflict into Canadian women's history' (p. 82). Fiske writes that understanding the discursive formation of Aboriginal women's sexuality 'requires us to build on the early work of Sylvia Van Kirk (1980) and Jennifer Brown (1980) by placing Aboriginal women in the context of the expectations held of settler women' (p. 12); this extends the work rather than rejecting it. Pierson's 'Colonization and Canadian Women's History' (1992) cites the book (OpenAlex reference list only; text unread). Criticism is recorded on rel_01 (Bowsfield) and rel_04 (LaRocque). edge_872 compares the two field entries at title level; this edge adds her own words and the field's reading of her.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Anthropological models brought to fur-trade, court and mission records for Métis, Cree and Ojibwe history (1983–96)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period, her own words. The 1983 essay (Canadian Journal of Native Studies 3:1, read in full) reads fur-trade sources through anthropological models. Bishop and Krech's argument for early subarctic 'matriorganization' leads her to ask 'whether native women in emergent metis groups looked for and found ways to maintain this organizational bias in their own families and social lives' (p. 40). She tests Asch's 'unilocality' among the Slavey against fur-trade families (p. 42), using the HBC district report on Île-à-la-Crosse of 1823 (p. 42) and the published Red River testimonies of 1818 (pp. 43–44). She presents women's studies as 'one important perspective, among several' (p. 40). Her presidential address to the American Society for Ethnohistory (Ethnohistory 38:2, 1991) is known through an indexed excerpt only, OpenAlex's abstract field; the page itself was not inspected. It speaks of 'the rather obscure niche occupied by our field, methodology, approach, or whatever it is we do when we do ethnohistory', and offers 'auto-ethnohistory' as 'a useful handle for some reflections about ethnohistory and ethnohistorians, myself included' (indexed excerpt; p. 113 is the recorded first page). Title-level: The Orders of the Dreamed (with Brightman, 1988), an edition of the trader George Nelson's 1823 account of Cree and Northern Ojibwa religion and myth, and Reading Beyond Words: Contexts for Native History (ed. with Vibert, 1996). Reception, read in full: Fiske (Atlantis 25:1, 2000) cites Brown and Vibert (1996) for the literary turn 'that subjects both oral and written narratives to textual analysis' (p. 13). McPherson (2000, n. 31) cites an essay in that volume as discursive analysis of a Red River trial. Gresko (1981) objected to the 'bits of anthropological theory' in Strangers in Blood (p. 113). Later readings, labelled. Brown (2012, read in the 2017 reprint) recalls that 'my courses and professors directed me towards broader issues of method and theory'. She also says she 'benefited from confronting the multiple problems around defining such categories as "marriage," "custom," and "society"' (pp. 191–92). The 2017 part introduction calls the pair 'I coming from anthropology and Sylvia from history' (p. 159). Her essay 'The Blind Men and the Elephant' (1990) is read only in its revised 2017 reprint, which cites a 2014 book. There she asks historians to 'start by deconstructing' the fur trade, and warns that subsuming northern Native history under 'the fur trade era' restricts it to 'certain rather specialized "Indian-White relations"' (pp. 63–65); the 1990 wording is unchecked. The edge claims a contribution to the field's documentary method, not that she shaped ethnohistory as a whole.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Joint conception of the Oxford History of the United States provides a shared editorial project.

Crossref DOI record (Ethnohistory 38:2, 1991, first page 113; last page not given). Indexed excerpt only: the abstract field of the OpenAlex record, which reproduces opening text of the address; neither the printed page nor the body (closed) was inspected. Passages: 'the rather obscure niche occupied by our field, methodology, approach, or whatever it is we do when we do ethnohistory'; 'auto-ethnohistory'; 'a useful handle for some reflections about ethnohistory and ethnohistorians, myself included'; Bill Simmons asked her in August 1988 'if I would be a candidate for president of the American Society for Ethnohistory'. Her predecessors as president, Axtell (1990) and Fogelson (1989), are named.

Open-access PDF from the publisher (aupress.ca, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0), 368 PDF pages. Read: acknowledgements (pp. vii–viii); part introduction (p. 159: 'I coming from anthropology and Sylvia from history, overlapping yet complementary'); chapter 3, 'The Blind Men and the Elephant' (pp. 61–66; revised reprint of a 1988 conference paper published 1990, citing Conrad Black 2014); chapter 9 opening (pp. 145–46: the title changed from 'The Presbyterian Métis of St. Gabriel Street' because 'the term "Métis," as used in Rupert's Land in the 1800s, referred particularly to Roman Catholics of French Canadian paternal origin' and the children 'cannot be subsumed under any one label'); chapter 11 (her 2012 essay); publication credits (pp. 345–47: 'In a few instances, chapter titles in this book have been somewhat modified from the originals').

Read in full in an Internet Archive capture (22 October 2023) of the journal PDF (cws.journals.yorku.ca/index.php/cws/article/download/14091/13144); the live York site is behind a bot check. The PDF is a two-page scan whose OJS record is titled for the next review on the page (Posner, 'Becoming a Mother'); the article page gives Vol 3, No 2 (1981), Book Reviews, dated 1981-06-01. Printed '112' and '113' read on a 300-dpi re-OCR. Passages: 'any relationship, even familial that the law refused to admit as legitimate'; 'one way of characterizing the meetings of Whites and Indians ... in the fur trade of North America'; 'their common British (and heavily Scottish) facade'; 'strongly related to changing economic pressures'; 'not to assume an active paternal role'; 'still too much in the form of the academic thesis'; 'complicated by seemingly insignificant bits of anthropological theory'; no mention of Jamieson's Indian Women and the Law in Canada (1978). A same-reviewer Atlantis record (6:2, 1981, pp. 213–14, 'Strangers In Blood') was also checked: its PDF holds Gresko's review of Light and Strong-Boag's True Daughters of the North, not of Brown.

Read in full in an Internet Archive capture (2016) of Brandon University's CJNS archive PDF; the live URL now returns 404. Running head 'THE CANADIAN JOURNAL OF NATIVE STUDIES III, 1(1983):39-46'; byline 'Department of Anthropology, University of Winnipeg'. The issue introduction says the papers were given at a Métis symposium in Winnipeg, 5–6 November 1982. OCR slips corrected ('coiling' to 'calling', 'contriburing' to 'contributing'). Passages: 'Biologically, métissage in North America can be described in a unitary way, as the meeting and mingling of Indian and white racial groups. Socially and culturally, it has had a complex history over many generations'; 'women's studies provide one important perspective, among several'; 'matriorganization'; 'Another starting point for this discussion is the work of Sylvia Van Kirk (1980)' (p. 40); 'patrifocality' (Brown 1980:218); 'by a margin of about two to one'; 'more likely by a two-to-one margin to remain in the Indian country' (p. 41); Asch's 'unilocality'; Île-à-la-Crosse 1823 (p. 42); 'were all in accord in calling attention to the maternal element as formative in metis emergence' (p. 44); 'It is all too easy to learn more about the men than the women' (p. 45). The references list Peterson and Brown, eds., The New Peoples, 'forthcoming', from the Newberry Library Conference on the Metis, Chicago, 1981.

Read in full in the journal PDF (article/download/10888/11811); author, date and pp. 121–126 from the article page metadata; issue from the page's issue link ('Archivaria 12', Summer 1981). Passages: 'constituted a social and cultural complex as well as an economic activity'; 'supports the claims of theorists in women's history that sex roles should constitute a category of historical investigation'; 'not a strident one'; 'This may be too complimentary a picture of both native women and European men'; 'using basically the same sources and employing the same macrobiographical approach as Van Kirk'; 'comparison between Hudson's Bay Company and North West Company men as husbands and fathers'; 'the relationship of hinterland to metropolis' (p. 124); 'With Van Kirk and Brown the unique and complex role of women and the fur trade family unit have been opened to investigation'; 'a distinctive Canadian approach to family history' (p. 126).

Read in full in the journal PDF (article/download/1542/1331); volume, issue, date and pp. 11–27 from the article page metadata. Pages by PDF order (17 pages for pp. 11–27).
